summary: Defines two new Mobile IP extensions that let equipment vendors and organizations add their own vendor or organization specific data. They are meant for research or deployment uses the standard does not cover.

plainLanguage.summary: It adds a blank box on a form where each company can write its own special notes.

questions: how to add custom data to mobile ip
what is mobile ip vendor specific extension
what is the difference between cvse and nvse
subtitle: Two Mobile IP extensions that let vendors and organizations carry their own private data in Mobile IP messages.

tldr.problem: The Mobile IP specification (RFC 2002) gave vendors and organizations no way to include their own specific information in Mobile IP messages.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3115 defines a Critical (CVSE) and a Normal (NVSE) Vendor/Organization Specific Extension. Each carries a vendor ID, a vendor-managed type and a free-form value.
tldr.outcome: Vendors can add private data for research or deployment, and the Critical/Normal split says what a receiver does when it does not understand the extension. It also fixes type numbers that differed between RFC 3025 and IANA.

today: RFC 3115 is a Proposed Standard and is not marked as obsoleted or updated in the metadata. It obsoletes RFC 3025.

sections.title: Why Vendor Extensions Were Needed
sections.content:
The Mobile IP specification, RFC 2002, does not allow organizations and vendors to include their own information in Mobile IP messages. With wide-scale deployment of Mobile IP imminent, RFC 3115 defines two extensions that vendors and organizations can use for their own purposes, for research or deployment.

An RFC Editor note explains that this memo corrects discrepancies between RFC 3025 and the IANA registry: RFC 3025 gave the critical type number as 37 and the normal one as 133, while IANA had 38 and 134. The memo obsoletes RFC 3025 because current implementations follow the IANA assignments.
sections.plainLanguage: A standard form had no space for companies to add their own notes. This gives them two kinds of note space.

sections.title: The CVSE and NVSE Formats
sections.content:
Both extensions are type-length-value items. The Critical Vendor/Organization Specific Extension (CVSE) uses type 38 and has a two-octet length field. The Normal Vendor/Organization Specific Extension (NVSE) uses type 134 and has a one-octet length field.

Each carries a Reserved field (for the CVSE it MUST be set to 0 on sending and ignored on reception) and a Vendor/Org-ID: the high-order octet is 0 and the low-order three octets are the vendor's SMI Network Management Private Enterprise Code in network byte order. Next comes a vendor-administered type (Vendor-CVSE-Type or Vendor-NVSE-Type) and a value of zero or more octets whose length is derived from the Length field.

Length counts the bytes of the extension, not including the Type and Length bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note has a company tag, a note-kind number that only that company understands, and then the note itself.

sections.title: What Receivers Do with Unknown Extensions
sections.content:
The difference between the two is what happens when one is not recognized. An unrecognized CVSE means the message MUST be silently discarded, in line with RFC 2002 rules for extension numbers 0 through 127. An unrecognized NVSE SHOULD be ignored, and the rest of the extensions and message data MUST still be processed.

If an entity recognizes the CVSE type but the vendor ID or vendor type inside is unsupported, a registration request gets a registration reject (or the appropriate deny message) with an error code for an unknown CVSE. For replies, a transit node (for example a foreign agent relaying a home agent's reply) MUST send a reject onward, while a non-transit node treats the reply as a reject. For an NVSE with an unknown vendor ID or type, the whole extension is skipped.

The RFC warns designers that a reply carrying a CVSE could be discarded by the entity processing it.
sections.plainLanguage: A 'must read' note you cannot understand makes the whole letter get thrown away. A 'nice to know' note you cannot understand is just skipped.

sections.title: Error Codes and Restrictions
sections.content:
Four error codes are defined. A foreign agent uses 100 for an unsupported vendor ID or uninterpretable CVSE sent by the mobile node, and 101 for one sent by the home agent. A home agent uses 140 for a CVSE from the mobile node and 141 for one from the foreign agent.

Multiple CVSE and NVSE items may appear in one message, anywhere after the fixed portion of the Mobile IP message. They are expected to be protected by the corresponding authenticator as necessary, and intermediate nodes should not change their ordering.
sections.plainLanguage: Each helper has its own 'I do not understand that company's note' code, depending on who sent the note.

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content:
IANA assigned the two extension type values from the numbering space for Mobile IP registration extensions, and assigned the four error codes from the foreign agent and home agent error code spaces.

On security, the RFC assumes Mobile IP messages are authenticated with a method defined by Mobile IP and imposes no additional requirements, so it is not expected to be a security issue.
sections.plainLanguage: The new notes follow the same safety rules as the rest of the form, so nothing new is needed.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to 0 on sending, ignored on reception.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Bytes of the extension, not including Type and Length.

fields.name: Vendor/Org-ID
fields.desc: High-order octet 0, low 3 octets the SMI Private Enterprise Code.

fields.name: Vendor-CVSE-Value
fields.desc: Zero or more octets of vendor data (continues).
